system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-11-17 00:15:00 to 2184-11-20 18:23:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis, gastrostomy, and a gastric pacemaker was admitted for severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Imaging revealed cecal volvulus with ischemia, likely caused by entanglement of the bowel with the pacemaker wires. She underwent an exploratory laparotomy, right hemicolectomy, ileotransverse anastomosis, stomach repair, and removal of the gastric pacemaker and wires. Postoperatively, she had ongoing nausea and difficulty tolerating oral intake, but gradually improved with tube feeds and diet advancement. A gastric emptying study was normal, but an upper GI series showed moderate esophageal dysmotility. She tolerated a regular diet and full tube feeds by discharge, with stable vital signs and healing incisions. She was discharged home with home health services for GJ tube care and follow-up with gastroenterology for esophageal evaluation.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with leukocytosis  // Is there pneumonia?

COMPARISON:  Radiographs from ___.

IMPRESSION: 

The feeding tube and right IJ central line have been removed. Surgical clips
are seen within the left axilla. Heart size is within normal limits. There is
tortuosity of the thoracic aorta. Lungs are clear. There are no
pneumothoraces. Degenerative changes are seen of the right glenohumeral joint.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with gastroparesis and GJ tube, requiring tube
replacement // Please replace tube

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to gj exchange performed ___.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure. Dr.
___ radiologist, personally supervised the trainee during the
key components of the procedure and reviewed and agreed with the trainee's
findings.
ANESTHESIA: Sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of 25 mcg of
fentanyl throughout the procedure  during which the patient's hemodynamic
parameters were continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology
nurse. 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Lidocaine, fentanyl
CONTRAST: 25 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 5.8 min, 20 mGy

PROCEDURE:  MIC gastrojejunostomy exchange.
PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.
The existing tube was injected with contrast and showed opacification of the
gastric rugae and duodenum. A guidewire was introduced into the stomach. The
existing feeding tube was then removed. A 16 ___ gastrojejunostomy catheter
was advanced over the wire into position. The sheath was then peeled away.
The catheters balloon was inflated with 7 ml of contrast contrast diluted in
sterile water in the stomach after confirming the position of the catheter
with a contrast injection. The catheter was then flushed, capped and secured
to the skin with a Stat Lock. Sterile dressings were applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Appropriately positioned new 16 ___ MIC gastrojejunostomy tube.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a gastrojejunostomy tube for a new 16 ___ MIC
gastrojejunostomy tube. The tube is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this pain for about two days now—diffuse, mostly in the lower belly. I’ve been nauseous and vomiting phlegm. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re not eating by mouth—you’re using your GJ tube for water and meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I haven’t taken anything by mouth in years. I’ve been trying crushed prochlorperazine and ondansetron, but they’re not helping this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve been using lorazepam and morphine for nausea and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I get really sedated. Still, the pain and nausea don’t go away. This feels like my usual gastroparesis flares, but worse and not responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned no diarrhea, fevers, or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, bowel movements are regular. No fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. In the ER, your white blood cell count was elevated—14.7—and you had some hematuria on urinalysis. But no signs of infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? The high white count?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we’re watching. But you don’t have fever or chills, and your blood cultures came back negative. So it may just be from inflammation or stress on the body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the CT scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT of your abdomen and pelvis showed no bowel obstruction or acute issue. No sign of another volvulus or blockage. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably just a bad gastroparesis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what it looks like. We’ll manage your symptoms and make sure nothing else develops. We’ve started IV morphine and acetaminophen for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But morphine makes my stomach slower. Could that be making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent point. That’s exactly why we’re planning to taper the morphine and switch to tramadol, which is gentler on gastric motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The pain is still there, but not as intense. Nausea is still bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reduced the IV morphine and started oral tramadol. We’re also continuing lorazepam for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to restart tube feeds? I’m worried about making nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted low-dose tube feeds this morning. So far, you’re tolerating them well. We’ll gradually increase as your symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my white count—is it still high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 14.7 on admission, but it’s coming down. Today it’s 11.2. No infection found, so we think it’s resolving on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray to check for pneumonia, since your white count was up. It was clear—no infection in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for checking. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re looking more comfortable today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Pain is mild now, and I haven’t vomited since yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your white count is now 9.8—back to normal. We’re keeping you on tramadol and acetaminophen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on lorazepam as needed. We’ve also added prochlorperazine for discharge, in case you need extra help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’d like to avoid morphine if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep it as a backup, but tramadol is safer for your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we had planned to replace your GJ tube this week. Since you’re here, interventional radiology can do it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot about that. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is due for replacement. It’s a quick procedure with sedation. They’ll use imaging to guide it and make sure it’s placed correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your GJ tube was successfully replaced this morning. The new one is in place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smoothly. You got a little fentanyl for sedation, and the radiologist confirmed placement with contrast. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. Your pain is well-controlled, nausea has improved, and labs are normal. You’re tolerating full tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medications am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your regular meds: citalopram, levothyroxine, omeprazole. For nausea, lorazepam and now prochlorperazine. For pain, tramadol every four hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you a small supply—10 tablets—for severe pain only. But try to avoid it, as it can slow your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please see your primary care provider this week to review everything and renew your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—was the leukocytosis ever explained?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No clear infection was found. We believe the elevated white count was due to inflammation from your gastroparesis flare. It resolved without antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thank you for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team has confirmed your tube feeds are running smoothly. You’re getting full strength and tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll keep that going at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Your vitals are stable—temperature 98.2, blood pressure 158/100, heart rate 88, oxygen 99% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: BP a bit high, but I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. Keep monitoring it at home. Otherwise, you’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea or pain returns and doesn’t respond to meds, or if you develop fever, vomiting, or tube issues, please call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’ll go home with home health services to help with GJ tube care for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you out shortly. Take care and get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis, GJ tube placement, and prior cecal volvulus presented with a two-day history of diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, consistent with a gastroparesis flare. She had elevated white blood cell count on admission but no signs of infection, and blood and urine cultures were negative. CT imaging showed no bowel obstruction or acute abdominal process. Pain was initially managed with IV morphine, but due to concerns about opioid-induced gastric slowing, she was transitioned to tramadol. Nausea was treated with lorazepam and tube feeds were successfully restarted. Her leukocytosis resolved spontaneously. As part of a planned outpatient procedure, her GJ tube was replaced by interventional radiology during the admission. She improved clinically, tolerated full tube feeds, and was discharged home with instructions to avoid opiates, continue new and home medications, and follow up with her primary care provider.
